_note: Text fields of project.json for the lead to merge (written by the write-ups builder). Numbers are left out on purpose: they live in README Results, generated from results/ and vendor/beacon/results/.
tagline: Pucks in a burning building hear the occupants' phones; each phone appears in the right room of a map built from the building's own data (record, aerial, 3D twin), drawn only as precisely as the measurement allows, and an AI command agent routes the rescue and writes the report.
abstract: When a commercial building is on fire, the incident commander's hardest question is who is still inside, and where. Sandtable Beacon is a command and reporting centre for that question. When the alarm comes in, an AI command agent reads three layers for the address (the building record with its tenants, the aerial image, the 3D twin) and writes the pre-incident plan. A crew places small pucks (Qorvo DWM3001CDK boards: Bluetooth and UWB) in the building. Occupants who opened an opt-in app are ranged through their phones, and each phone is drawn as what the measurement supports: a ring, two candidate points, or one point, in the right room and beside who the building record expects there. The agent prioritises, routes a rescue crew through the twin, issues the radio order and writes the report the command post keeps. The same code has run privately on live CoStar, Matterport and Vexcel data for one real building; this repository runs on labelled stand-ins, and phones, pucks and crews are simulated.
aha: Two pucks give each phone two possible places, mirror images of each other; the building's own walls rule one out, so phone 1 lands as a point in the suite while phone 2 honestly stays 'two places: search both'. Then the record against the phones: the record says who should be in that suite, the phones say who is (on a live record, possibly 'the record says this suite is empty; the phones say three people are in it').
how_it_works: Pre-plan: a tool-using agent reads the building record (CoStar layer), the aerial image (Vexcel layer, through a vision tool) and the 3D twin (Matterport layer)
Pucks in: DWM3001CDK boards on stock firmware, positions tape-measured and clicked onto the plan; opt-in iPhones range them and report status (lane L16's Beacon module)
Drawn honestly: one puck a ring, two pucks two candidates, the twin deletes impossible ones, a point only for a fix; no app means a device count, never people
Accountability: the record's tenants and expected occupancy per suite set against the phones heard, as ranges
Command: the agent prioritises, routes a crew through the twin, radios the order, re-routes when a phone's geometry improves, requests EMS
Report and feeds: a printable command-post report, GeoJSON and Cursor-on-Target
stack: Claude via the Anthropic SDK, the Claude CLI, or replay of recorded real runs (claude-sonnet-5-5 recordings)
Lane L16 Beacon module (vendor/beacon): locator, tracker, simulator, iOS app (Apple Nearby Interaction)
Qorvo DWM3001CDK on stock Nearby Interaction firmware
Bench uwb-kit (vendor/uwbkit) for the simulated Crews mode
Scout radar simulator and DSP adapted from lane L08
Public open data: LA County assessor and LARIAC, City of LA business listings and GeoHub, US Census TIGERweb, USDA NAIP

sponsor_tech.costar: Building record: tenants by suite and floor, available spaces, employees, construction, stories; drives who-should-be-where in the accountability table and the agent's priorities. Ran privately live from the CoStar hackathon data kit for one real 12-storey building (26 property fields, 72 current tenant rows, 18 available spaces); the public repository runs on real open data for a different building, labelled as not CoStar's.
sponsor_tech.matterport: 3D twin: rooms, walls, doorways, walking graph; routes the crew and prunes impossible phone candidates. Ran privately live through the Model API for one scanned suite (8 rooms, 48 walls, 14 doorways, 30 scan positions, 199-edge graph), Showcase SDK view on localhost; public repository: a synthetic twin fitted to the stand-in footprint.
sponsor_tech.vexcel: Aerial: sides of the building, approach, staging; the agent looks at the image through a vision tool. Ran privately live through API v2 (7 images: orthos, a roof detail, four obliques); public repository: real USDA NAIP imagery as the stand-in.
sponsor_tech.anthropic: Claude as the command agent (tool use in a plan, act, re-plan loop); stand-in runs replay recorded real responses; the private live run used a live model.

rubric.Use of the data (30%): Record says who should be in each suite (and which suites are available); twin gives rooms, routes and deletes impossible phone positions (two pucks become one point); aerial gives sides, approach and staging read by a vision tool; ran privately on all three live layers for one real building, publicly on labelled stand-ins.
rubric.Agentic depth (30%): Situations as goals with a reply budget; the agent chooses tools (record, aerial vision, twin, phones, accountability) and ends in actions (assign with route, radio, EMS request, observations, record corrections); must search a ring or two candidates, never 'go to the phone'; on the stand-in all three exercises replay recorded real model turns with no fallback (results/replay_check_*_auto_3A2T.json).
rubric.Usefulness (25%): Incident commander and command post: who is inside, where, who is unaccounted for as an honest range, and a report at the end; prevention bureaus get a pre-plan draft for any commercial address.
rubric.Demo and polish (15%): One screen, two physical pucks and two iPhones, a printable report, a phone page for the rescue team that reads the feed; every uncertain thing drawn as uncertain.

limitations: Not run on hardware: no phone and no puck has been in the loop of any result; lane L16's iOS source has not been built or run here; the real range error of an iPhone against these boards is unmeasured

Opt-in only: a phone without the app is never ranged or identified; the most a puck could give is a Bluetooth device count (the simulated pucks show one, the stock puck firmware cannot collect it), and devices are not people; the app must stay open with the screen on as built
Two pucks often leave two candidates; the twin removes one only when the geometry allows
The public repository holds no sponsor data: its twin is synthetic, so walls that prune a candidate there are plausible, not real

The private live run covered one scanned suite, not the storey; the scan's georeference lands about 90 m from the record's map point (flagged, not corrected); its first run needed one order given by hand (fixed since)
Life hazards and expected head counts are inferences and estimates from the record

Privacy as built: this board keeps what it received for the incident report and serves /api/beacons and /api/report without authentication on the local network; stop-sharing deletion and 15-minute retention exist in lane L16's module only; the rotating phone id is a design, not implemented
Scout (radar) and Crews (tags) are simulation-only on these boards; the radar simulator was written alongside its detector
One floor modelled; not a life-safety product

self_score_reasons.creativity: Using the building's own walls to decide between two possible phone positions, and setting the record against the phones, are new uses of CoStar-style data; phones as a rescue sensor is not new in itself
self_score_reasons.utility: Runs end to end hands-free with a real report and feeds, and ran privately on live sponsor data; nothing has run on the boards or phones
self_score_reasons.charity: Finding trapped people sooner is a real public good, but the Healthcare fit is the pre-hospital end only, with no clinical content
self_score_reasons.avidity: Three sensing modes, a reporting centre, a private live run on three layers, a puck enclosure, a sourced feasibility answer and honest labels throughout
self_score_reasons.track_fit: CoStar: all three layers used together and agentically, live in private; hardware and physical AI are not met until something runs on the boards
self_score_reasons.demo_risk: The hands-free stand-in run is safe; live mode depends on the owner's laptop and keys, and hardware has not been brought up

images.caption: Hands-free beacon run (simulated phones, pucks and crews; replayed recorded agent turns): two pucks placed by hand in Suite 310; phone B1's second possible place is a mirror image across the line between the pucks and falls outside the building, so the twin rules it out and B1 is a point.
The same run a moment later: B1 a point, B2 still two places inside Suite 310 that the twin cannot choose between; the agent orders a search. Simulated, replayed turns.
Engine 1's phone page in the hands-free run: the order to search for B2 (one of 2 places in Suite 310), what the occupant typed, and the located people read from the GeoJSON feed. Simulated.

The reporting centre (/report.html) after the hands-free beacon run on the stand-in building (simulated phones, pucks and crews; replayed recorded agent turns): the plan of the floor with each phone's last place, B1's mirror place ruled out because it is outside the building, B2's other place ruled out by Engine 1's search, the two pucks and the line through them.
The Beacon puck enclosure for one DWM3001CDK and a cell: a self-righting ball, designed and checked in software, not printed.
The owner's radar question: how 1, 2, 3 and 5 pucks constrain one target (geometry only). Scout mode is simulation only.
